advances: Proves the proposed entropy lower bound, with an integral coordinatewise rounding witness in the mean fiber. For a totally unimodular catalog of grouped signed Bernoulli or shifted two-Bernoulli contributions, it gives the explicit original-capacity coefficient bound \(\prod_j(2m_j+1)^{-1}\). The bound can transfer conditional-event estimates back to the original probability law. An exact non-TU example shows that an integer projected mean need not even belong to the image support without the matrix hypothesis.

proof:
First suppose \(t>0\). Each \(\mu_j\) lies in \([l_j,u_j]\), because it is an average of points in that interval. Since the endpoints are integers, both \(\lfloor\mu_j\rfloor\) and \(\lceil\mu_j\rceil\) lie in the same interval. In particular, all the rounding-box integer points used below belong to the actual positive support.

For \(l_j<u_j\), define \(\varphi_j\) by linearly interpolating the values \(\log p_j(k)\) between successive integer support points. Its slope on \([k,k+1]\) is \(\log p_j(k+1)-\log p_j(k)\). Taking logarithms of the log-concavity inequalities shows that these successive slopes are nonincreasing. Hence \(\varphi_j\) is concave: at any point of the interval, a slope between the left and right slopes gives an affine upper supporting function on the whole interval, because all slopes to its left are no smaller and all slopes to its right are no larger. At an endpoint, use the adjacent slope. Applying this supporting inequality at \(\mu_j\) and averaging it over \(Y_j\) makes the linear term vanish, giving

\[
\varphi_j(\mu_j)
\ge \mathbb E\varphi_j(Y_j)
=\sum_{k=l_j}^{u_j}p_j(k)\log p_j(k)
=-H(Y_j).
\]

If \(l_j=u_j\), then \(Y_j=l_j\) surely, \(p_j(l_j)=1\), and \(H(Y_j)=0\). Set \(\varphi_j(l_j)=0\); the same inequality holds on this one-point domain.

We next give the determinant proof of the required integrality, including existence of an optimal vertex. Let \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb Z^t\) be any finite coordinate bounds with \(\alpha\le\beta\), and suppose the bounded polytope \(P_{\alpha,\beta}=\{x\in\mathbb R^t:Bx=b,\ \alpha\le x\le\beta\}\) is nonempty. It is closed and bounded, so any affine objective \(L\) attains its maximum there. Among maximizers, choose \(x\) for which the number of coordinates at a bound is largest. This choice exists, because those counts form a nonempty finite set of integers.

Let \(I=\{j:\alpha_j<x_j<\beta_j\}\). If the columns of \(B\) indexed by \(I\) were linearly dependent, there would be a nonzero vector \(v\), supported on \(I\), with \(Bv=0\). Both \(x+sv\) and \(x-sv\) are feasible for all sufficiently small positive \(s\). Since \(x\) maximizes the affine objective, its linear coefficient in direction \(v\) must be zero; otherwise one of these two points would improve it. Moving from \(x\) in the positive \(v\) direction until the first coordinate reaches a bound is possible: \(v\ne0\), all its affected coordinates start strictly inside finite intervals, and the first hitting time is the minimum of their positive times to the appropriate bound. The resulting point remains feasible, retains the same objective value, fixes every previously fixed coordinate, and adds at least one coordinate at a bound. This contradicts the choice of \(x\). Thus the columns \(B_{\cdot I}\) are linearly independent.

This also proves that \(x\) is a vertex. Indeed, if \(x\) is a convex combination of two feasible points with both weights positive, its bound coordinates force the corresponding coordinates of both points to coincide with those of \(x\). Their difference is consequently supported on \(I\) and is annihilated by \(B\). Column independence forces that difference to be zero. Conversely, dependent free columns at a vertex would give two distinct feasible points \(x+sv,x-sv\) with midpoint \(x\), a contradiction. Thus every vertex of \(P_{\alpha,\beta}\) has independent columns indexed by its strictly interior coordinates.

For any such vertex, let \(k=|I|\). If \(k=0\), all its coordinates are integer bounds. If \(k>0\), the rows of \(B_{\cdot I}\) span \(\mathbb R^k\): otherwise a nonzero vector orthogonal to their span would give a linear dependence among its columns. Choose \(k\) basis rows, indexed by \(J\). The square matrix \(B_{J,I}\) therefore has nonzero determinant. All coordinates in \(I^c\) are integer bounds, so the vertex satisfies

\[
B_{J,I}x_I=b_J-B_{J,I^c}x_{I^c}\in\mathbb Z^k.
\]

TU and nonsingularity give \(\det B_{J,I}\in\{1,-1\}\). Cramer's rule expresses each coordinate of \(x_I\) as an integer determinant, obtained by replacing one column by the displayed integer right-hand side, divided by \(1\) or \(-1\). Every coordinate is therefore integral. This proves integrality of every vertex and of the selected affine maximizer, without augmenting the matrix or assuming any particular rank of \(B\).

Apply this conclusion with \(\alpha_j=\lfloor\mu_j\rfloor\) and \(\beta_j=\lceil\mu_j\rceil\). The point \(\mu\) belongs to \(P_{\alpha,\beta}\), since \(B\mu=b\), so the polytope is nonempty. On each nondegenerate coordinate interval \([\alpha_j,\beta_j]\), the endpoints are consecutive integers, and \(\varphi_j\) is affine there. On a fixed coordinate it is constant. Consequently \(\sum_j\varphi_j(x_j)\) is the restriction of an affine function to this box. The preceding argument supplies an integral maximizer \(y\) in the polytope. It follows that

\[
\sum_j\log p_j(y_j)
=\sum_j\varphi_j(y_j)
\ge\sum_j\varphi_j(\mu_j)
\ge-\sum_j H(Y_j).
\]

Exponentiating and using independence gives \(\mathbb P(Y=y)=\prod_jp_j(y_j)\ge\exp(-\sum_jH(Y_j))\). Since \(By=b\), the event \(\{Y=y\}\) is contained in \(\{BY=b\}\), proving the first probability bound.

For the range bound, put \(N_j=u_j-l_j+1\). The elementary inequality \(\log z\le z-1\) for \(z>0\) follows, for example, by differentiating \(z-1-\log z\), whose minimum is zero at \(z=1\). Apply it to \(z=1/(N_jp_j(k))\), multiply by \(p_j(k)\), and sum over the \(N_j\) support points. The result is \(H(Y_j)-\log N_j\le\sum_k(1/N_j-p_j(k))=0\). Thus \(\exp(-H(Y_j))\ge1/N_j\), and multiplying proves the second bound.

All fixed coordinates, including singleton supports and integral means, were already included in the determinant argument. Rank deficiency causes no issue, because only the independent free columns require a square minor. For \(r=0\), the unique empty projected vector is \(b\), and \(BY=b\) occurs surely; the same box argument applies. If \(t=0\), then \(Y\), \(\mu\), and \(y\) are the unique empty vectors, \(b=B\mu=0\in\mathbb Z^r\), and the displayed chain reads \(1\ge1=1\ge1\ge1\). This verifies the remaining boundary case.

We prove the group-law assertions rather than invoking convolution closure. Let \((p_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z}\) be a positive log-concave probability sequence on a finite integer interval, extended by zero, and let an independent Bernoulli variable have success probability \(\theta\in[0,1]\). The mass after adding it is \(q_k=(1-\theta)p_k+\theta p_{k-1}\). Direct expansion gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
q_k^2-q_{k-1}q_{k+1}
={}&(1-\theta)^2(p_k^2-p_{k-1}p_{k+1})
+\theta^2(p_{k-1}^2-p_{k-2}p_k)\\
&+\theta(1-\theta)(p_kp_{k-1}-p_{k-2}p_{k+1}).
\end{aligned}
\]

The first two parentheses are nonnegative by log-concavity. For the last one, if \(p_{k-2}p_{k+1}=0\), nonnegativity is immediate. Otherwise all four indices belong to the positive interval support. Multiplying \(p_{k-1}^2\ge p_{k-2}p_k\) and \(p_k^2\ge p_{k-1}p_{k+1}\), then dividing by \(p_{k-1}p_k>0\), gives \(p_kp_{k-1}\ge p_{k-2}p_{k+1}\). Hence \(q\) is log-concave. For \(0<\theta<1\), its support is the positive interval from the old lower endpoint to one beyond the old upper endpoint. For \(\theta=0\) or \(1\), it is respectively the old law or its integer translate.

Starting with the point mass at zero, this proves by induction that every sum of independent Bernoulli variables has positive log-concave mass on its actual interval support. A negative Bernoulli contribution can be written \(-Z=(1-Z)-1\); the variable \(1-Z\) is Bernoulli, with success probability \(1-\mathbb P(Z=1)\). Thus any signed sum is an integer translate of a sum of independent Bernoulli variables. Integer translation preserves the inequalities and positivity of interval support. Replacing variables by these individual functions also preserves independence, as is seen by summing their product joint mass over the corresponding preimages.

Every nondegenerate Bernoulli trial increases the support width by one, while deterministic trials only translate the law. Therefore a sum with at most \(m_j\) signed trials has width at most \(m_j\), and a sum with at most \(2m_j\) signed trials has width at most \(2m_j\). This includes \(m_j=0\), when the group is a point mass. Groups are independent because they depend on disjoint independent trial blocks: summing the joint product trial mass over specified values of the group sums factors into the product of the individual group masses. The main theorem therefore applies to the group variables. Since \(u_j-l_j+1\le2m_j+1\), it yields the claimed original-capacity lower bound, and the first-form bound follows in the same way.

For catalog TU inheritance, any square submatrix of the retained, possibly negated columns is a square submatrix of the original matrix with some columns multiplied by \(-1\). Its determinant is the original determinant times a sign, so it still belongs to \(\{0,1,-1\}\). The grouping interpretation \(BY=\sum_jB_{\cdot j}Y_j\) simply absorbs the signs of original contributions along a representative vector into the group variables. Finally, the mean fiber has positive probability by the theorem, so \(\mathbb P(A\mid F_b)\) is defined. The conditional-probability identity and the established bounds prove the stated transfer inequality. This argument imposes no hypothesis on the conditional groups or on the multivariate image mass function.

In the separating example, \(\det B=-2\), so \(B\) is not TU. Each fair Bernoulli law is positive and log-concave on \([0,1]\cap\mathbb Z\), and each entropy is \(\log2\). The mean is \(\mu=(1/2,1/2)^{\mathsf T}\), giving \(b=B\mu=(1,0)^{\mathsf T}\). The four equally likely inputs \((0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)\) have respective images \((0,0),(1,1),(1,-1),(2,0)\). None is \(b\). Equivalently, the equations \(y_1+y_2=1\) and \(y_1-y_2=0\) force \(y_1=y_2=1/2\), which is not an integer input. Thus \(\mathbb P(BY=b)=0<1/4=\exp(-H(Y_1)-H(Y_2))\), completing the exact non-TU verification.
statement:
Let \(t,r\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). For each \(j\in\{1,\ldots,t\}\), let \(l_j,u_j\in\mathbb Z\) with \(l_j\le u_j\), and let \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_t\) be independent integer-valued random variables. Write \(p_j(k)=\mathbb P(Y_j=k)\). Assume that \(p_j(k)>0\) exactly for \(k\in[l_j,u_j]\cap\mathbb Z\), and that the zero-extended sequence satisfies \(p_j(k)^2\ge p_j(k-1)p_j(k+1)\) for every integer \(k\). All logarithms are natural, and \(H(Y_j)=-\sum_{k=l_j}^{u_j}p_j(k)\log p_j(k)\).

Let \(Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_t)^{\mathsf T}\), \(\mu=\mathbb EY\), and let \(B\in\mathbb Z^{r\times t}\) be totally unimodular, meaning that every square submatrix has determinant in \(\{0,1,-1\}\). Suppose that \(b=B\mu\in\mathbb Z^r\). Then there is \(y\in\mathbb Z^t\) such that \(By=b\) and \(\lfloor\mu_j\rfloor\le y_j\le\lceil\mu_j\rceil\) for every \(j\), and

\[
\mathbb P(BY=b)
\ge \mathbb P(Y=y)
=\prod_{j=1}^t p_j(y_j)
\ge \exp\!\left(-\sum_{j=1}^t H(Y_j)\right)
\ge \prod_{j=1}^t\frac{1}{u_j-l_j+1}.
\]

There is no full-row-rank assumption and no additional factor depending on \(r\). Zero rows, redundant constraints, singleton supports, \(r=0\), and \(t=0\) are allowed. Empty sums and products are respectively zero and one.

Notation and normalization map: the assignment's interpolant \(h_j\) is denoted \(\varphi_j\) in this proof. It is unrelated to the locked problem's unnormalized halfspace depth \(h_S\). Here \(\mathbb P\) is the original normalized product probability law, before conditioning, and \(y\in\mathbb Z^t\) is an auxiliary rounding witness, not a claimed point of the locked set \(S\). For the locked problem with \(\mathcal H_d(S)>0\), the probability normalization is exactly \(A\mapsto\mathcal H_d(S\cap A)/\mathcal H_d(S)\), and the corresponding normalized depth is \(h_S(\mathbf y)/\mathcal H_d(S)\). No identification of that volume law with this auxiliary product law is assumed.

The following catalog application is also part of the statement. Let \(m_j\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) be the original number of contributions in group \(j\), let \(c_j\in\mathbb Z\), and let every underlying Bernoulli variable be independent of every other underlying Bernoulli variable, with success probabilities allowed anywhere in \([0,1]\). A group variable may have either form

\[
Y_j=c_j+\sum_{a=1}^{m_j}\varepsilon_{j,a}Z_{j,a},
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
Y_j=c_j+\sum_{a=1}^{m_j}
\left(\varepsilon_{j,a}^{(1)}Z_{j,a}^{(1)}
+\varepsilon_{j,a}^{(2)}Z_{j,a}^{(2)}\right),
\]

where every sign is in \(\{-1,1\}\). The second form includes sums of ternary contributions \(Z^{(1)}+Z^{(2)}-1\) or \(Z^{(1)}-Z^{(2)}\), by choosing the integer shift and signs appropriately. Each group law has positive log-concave mass on its actual integer support interval. Its support width \(u_j-l_j\) is at most \(m_j\) in the first form and at most \(2m_j\) in the second form. Thus “width at most \(2m_j\)” means at most \(2m_j+1\) integer support points.

Let the integer catalog vectors be the columns of a TU matrix \(B\), so the coupled constraint is \(BY=\sum_j B_{\cdot j}Y_j=b\). Whenever \(b=B\mathbb EY\) is integral, the displayed theorem applies and gives \(\mathbb P(BY=b)\ge\prod_j(2m_j+1)^{-1}\). For groups of the first form only, the stronger denominator \(\prod_j(m_j+1)^{-1}\) applies. The capacities \(m_j\) are these original contribution counts; they are not replaced by support widths or by conditional multiplicities. If the catalog is obtained from a TU matrix by retaining one representative of each class of columns equal up to sign, and optionally negating representatives, it is itself TU.

Writing \(F_b=\{BY=b\}\), for every event \(A\) under this original law one consequently has

\[
\mathbb P(A\cap F_b)
=\mathbb P(F_b)\mathbb P(A\mid F_b)
\ge \exp\!\left(-\sum_j H(Y_j)\right)\mathbb P(A\mid F_b)
\ge \left(\prod_j\frac{1}{2m_j+1}\right)\mathbb P(A\mid F_b).
\]

The entropies in this expression are those of the unconditioned independent groups. No independence or log-concavity of the conditioned groups, and no log-concavity of the full image mass function \(z\mapsto\mathbb P(BY=z)\), is asserted.

Finally, TU cannot simply be omitted, even for matrices with entries in \(\{0,1,-1\}\). For \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\) and two independent fair Bernoulli variables, \(B\mathbb EY=(1,0)^{\mathsf T}\) is integral but has probability zero under \(BY\), whereas \(\exp(-H(Y_1)-H(Y_2))=1/4\).
